newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN refugee body protests Bangladesh expulsions.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee body protests Bangladesh expulsions.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR protested to Bangladesh on Wednesday over the expulsions of Burmese refugees and warned it might cut back its activities there unless the policy was changed.
The protest, sent to Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad by UNHCR's Assistant High Commissioner Sergio Vieira de Mello, followed the forcible repatriation of 399 Burmese Moslems on Sunday and Tuesday.

The operations sparked off clashes between riot police and refugees in camps just inside Bangladesh's south-eastern border in which several people were injured. De Mello's letter, according to UNHCR, said they violated international law.

"We have also received reports of maltreatment of refugees during the preparation for their return, including physical abuse, the separation of at least 67 minors from their mothers, and the return of individuals who are ill or handicapped and therefore unfit for repatriation without medical supervision," it declared.
Some 21,000 Burmese Moslems, known as Rohingas, are left in Bangladesh out of nearly 250,000 who fled across the border in the early 1990s.

Many said they were fleeing persecution by Burma's military rulers. But the Bangladesh government argues they are economic migrants who place a heavy burden on the economy of one of the world's least-developed countries.

Nearly 230,000 of the original refugees have returned under voluntary repatriation programmes supervised by the UNHCR. But the refugee agency says that aside from those still left behind, more are now crossing over from Burma.

In his letter, de Mello appealed to the government in Dacca to halt all forced repatriations and allow the U.N. agency to interview any returnees to ensure they were going back of their own free will.

"In the absence of such arrangements," it said, "the UNHCR would no longer be in a position to associate itself with the repatriation operation" under which most of the earlier refugees had gone back home voluntarily.

The UNHCR said tension had been rising in refugee camps amid reports of a further roundup and forced return on Thursday. In one camp at a location called Nayapara, refugees had refused their food rations for the past four days and locked themselves in their huts.

Some said they would prefer to starve rather than return to Burma, a statement from the agency said. In another camp, it added, several hundred Rohingas were involved earlier on Wednesday in a tense stand-off with police.
